610.title: Guru Tegh Bahadur's bani close
610.howItsDone: Sikhs hear Guru Tegh Bahadur's shabads in kirtan and his saloks at every bhog, and on the day of his martyrdom, often observed in November or December, gurdwaras sing his bani and tell the story of Delhi.

segments.voice: Yesterday: bhog, and your line: read for the departed. Today we close a whole stretch: thirty-two days with the ninth Guru.

If you had to describe a teacher in four words after a month with them, what would you pick? Not their biography. The feel of them: the voice you'd hear in your head when you needed it. We started this block on the ninth Guru's voice, calm and plain. Since then we've walked through his shabads in their ragas and all fifty-seven saloks. A wall of sand. Friends in good times. Kanchan. Fear none, frighten none. Auadh. Rama gone, Ravana gone. Strength gone, strength returned. Rahio. Before we turn to the Ardas, four words for the whole of it.
screen: `FOUR WORDS FOR A TEACHER.` → `A MONTH WITH THE NINTH GURU.` → `BEFORE WE TURN TO THE ARDAS.`

segments.voice: The four words are calm, fearless, detached, and kind. Calm. His bani has almost no drama in it. Short lines, plain words, the same truths said again and again: live in the world, shining, like a dream, auadh. It reads like someone speaking slowly to a friend who is upset. Fearless. The salok we met as fear none, frighten none says, in paraphrase, that the wise one gives fear to no one, and accepts fear from no one. Sikhs see that line lived out in his death. Tradition remembers that he went to Delhi and gave his life in 1675, and Sikhs honor him as having died for others' freedom to practice their own faith. He's often called Hind di chadar, the shield of India. Detached. The word in his bani is often bairaag, a turning away from clutching, and the picture is kanchan and iron alike, praise and blame alike. Not cold, but unhooked: love without clutching, as one day's line had it. Kind. This one is easy to miss, because his bani talks so much about death. But all that talk of passing is never meant to frighten. It's said the way you'd tell someone you love: we don't have forever, so let's not waste it. Strength gone, then strength returned. All companions gone, then rahio. Every hard line turns, sooner or later, toward what stays. That's the ninth Guru's bani: fifty-nine shabads in fifteen ragas, and fifty-seven saloks, most of them two lines long. Small in size. Not small in weight.
screen: `CALM: PLAIN LINES, SAID SLOWLY.` · `FEARLESS: FEAR NONE, FRIGHTEN NONE.` · `DETACHED: GOLD AND IRON ALIKE.` · `KIND: EVERY HARD LINE TURNS.` · then, large: `CALM AND FEARLESS.`

segments.voice: Let a few of this month's lines pass through your mind: live in the world, shining; like a dream; nothing stays; today or tomorrow; only you; the Name remains; nothing equals it. Don't choose the wisest; notice the one that tugs, and say it three times, slowly, with your breath. If you pray, follow it with Waheguru.
Nirbhau, without fear. One of four words for his bani: calm, nirbhau, detached, and kind: fifty-nine shabads and fifty-seven saloks, small in size, not small in weight.
Your line: calm and fearless. Tomorrow, the prayer said standing. Day six hundred ten, and a whole block done.

611.title: The standing prayer
611.hook: Ardas is prayed standing, hands folded, at the start and end of everything
611.howItsDone: Sikhs say the Ardas standing with folded hands, facing the Guru Granth Sahib where it is present, at the end of services and at the start and end of any important undertaking, with the sangat answering Waheguru.

segments.voice: Yesterday: nirbhau, and your line: calm and fearless, four words for the ninth Guru's bani. Today a new block begins: the Ardas, line by line.

At the end of a gurdwara service, the whole room does the same thing. Everyone who was sitting cross-legged on the floor gets up. They stand, face the Guru Granth Sahib, and fold their hands in front of them. One person starts speaking, steady and rhythmic, and every so often the whole room answers in one word: Waheguru. You'll see the same thing at a wedding, before a new business opens, before a long journey, beside a hospital bed, at a funeral, before a meal is served from the langar, and after. It's the Sikh prayer for everything.
screen: `THE WHOLE ROOM STANDS.` → `HANDS FOLDED, FACING THE GURU.` → `THE PRAYER FOR EVERYTHING.`

segments.voice: It's called Ardas. Sikh tradition explains the word through the Persian arz-dasht: a petition, a written request, the kind handed up to a king. Heard that way, the name says what the Ardas is: a petition to God, made standing, the way you'd stand before someone you honor. It isn't one of the hymns of the Guru Granth Sahib. It grew up in the community, and its standard form is set out in the Sikh code of conduct, the Rehat Maryada. Over the coming weeks we'll go through it line by line. For now, here's the shape, in three movements. First, it opens with lines from Guru Gobind Singh's Var Sri Bhagauti Ji Ki, remembering God's power and the Gurus by name. Second, it remembers: the Guru Granth Sahib, the Panj Pyare, the Sahibzade, the martyrs, the gurdwaras, the long history of the community. Third, it asks: for the Name, for faith, for the good of the whole Khalsa, and then for whatever this particular moment needs, a wedding, a journey, a recovery. Then it closes by asking for the good of everyone. Notice that order. Before asking for anything, the Ardas remembers. By the time the request comes, you've been reminded who you stand with. And the room keeps answering, Waheguru, so the prayer is never one person's alone. The opening and the remembering stay much the same everywhere; the ask at the end changes with the occasion. It carries the whole history of the community, and room for this one Tuesday.
screen: `ARDAS: A PETITION, MADE STANDING.` · `FIRST, IT OPENS WITH THE GURUS.` · `NEXT, IT REMEMBERS THE COMMUNITY.` · `LAST, IT ASKS, FOR TODAY TOO.` · then, large: `STAND AND ASK.`

segments.voice: If you can, stand with your feet steady and your hands folded in front of you, and notice whether standing feels different from sitting, as if someone were in front of you. If you pray, ask God for one thing you need today in your own plain words, and end with Waheguru. If you don't, name silently one thing you hope for, for yourself and for someone else.
Ardas. A petition, made standing with folded hands: first it remembers, then it asks.
Your line: stand and ask. The whole room stands and answers with you. See you tomorrow.

612.title: The opening greeting
612.hook: it begins with Ik Onkar and the Khalsa's greeting to Waheguru
612.howItsDone: The Ardas begins with Ik Onkar, Waheguru ji ki fateh, and Sikhs greet one another with Waheguru ji ka Khalsa, Waheguru ji ki fateh, at meetings, in speeches and in letters.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ardas, the standing prayer, and your line: stand and ask. It remembers first, then asks. Today, the Ardas's very first words.

Two Sikhs meet at an airport, strangers, and one says: Waheguru ji ka Khalsa. The other answers right away: Waheguru ji ki fateh. They've never met, but in a handful of words they've placed each other. It's the Khalsa's greeting, which Sikh tradition traces to Guru Gobind Singh, used at the start of a speech, the end of a letter, the top of a wedding card. Half of it, with one small symbol in front, is also how the Ardas begins. Before the prayer remembers anyone or asks for anything, it says who the victory belongs to.
screen: `TWO STRANGERS AT AN AIRPORT.` → `A FEW WORDS, AND THEY KNOW.` → `HOW THE ARDAS BEGINS.`

segments.voice: The Ardas opens: Ik Onkar, Waheguru ji ki fateh. Ik Onkar is the very first word of the Guru Granth Sahib: the numeral one joined to the sign for Onkar. One God, everywhere, flowing through everything. Then Waheguru, the wondrous Guru, a name for God. Ji is respect, like saying sir or dear. And fateh is victory. The grammar is worth a second look. Waheguru ji ki fateh doesn't quite say victory to Waheguru, like a cheer. It says the victory is Waheguru's: the victory belongs to God. The first half of the full greeting says the same about the community: Waheguru ji ka Khalsa, the Khalsa belongs to Waheguru. So the line often rendered victory to Waheguru carries the sense that the victory is already Waheguru's. The greeting hands everything over. The community isn't ours; it's God's. The victory isn't ours; it's God's. Putting it at the head of the Ardas does the same work. Whatever the prayer goes on to ask, a good marriage, a safe flight, a recovery, the first thing said is: if anything goes well, the victory is God's. That takes some weight off. It also takes some pride off. The same heading, Ik Onkar, Waheguru ji ki fateh, stands at the top of Guru Gobind Singh's Var Sri Bhagauti Ji Ki, where the Ardas's next lines come from. So the greeting is like the letterhead on a page: the first thing you see, telling you whose house you're in.
screen: `IK ONKAR: ONE, EVERYWHERE.` · `WAHEGURU JI: THE WONDROUS GURU.` · `FATEH: THE VICTORY IS GOD'S.` · `THE LETTERHEAD ON THE PAGE.` · then, large: `VICTORY TO WAHEGURU.`

segments.voice: Sit or stand comfortably, and say the words slowly, aloud or silently, a few times: Ik Onkar, Waheguru ji ki fateh. Each time, notice what you're handing over: whatever goes well today, the victory isn't yours to carry. If you don't pray, sit with the idea instead: a success that doesn't need your pride.
Fateh, victory. Ik Onkar, Waheguru ji ki fateh: one God everywhere, and the fateh belongs to the wondrous Guru.
Your line: victory to waheguru. The credit goes where the victory belongs. Day six hundred twelve.

613.title: First, remember the Power
613.hook: the opening lines, from the Tenth Guru's Chandi di Var, remember the Divine as Bhagauti, the power of the sword
613.howItsDone: Every Ardas opens with the first stanza of Guru Gobind Singh's Var Sri Bhagauti Ji Ki, remembering Bhagauti and then the Gurus; Sikhs say it standing, often in a strong, rhythmic voice.

segments.voice: Yesterday: fateh, and your line: victory to waheguru; the victory is God's. Today, the first full line of the Ardas, and a word readers still discuss.

Before a sprinter settles into the blocks, there's a moment where she isn't thinking about the race at all. She's gathering something. Before a surgeon makes the first cut, before a firefighter goes up the ladder, there's that same breath. Not a plan. A summoning of strength from somewhere deeper than the plan. The Ardas has a moment like that right at its start. After the greeting, before naming a single Guru, it remembers a power. And the word it uses for that power has been argued over by readers for a long time.
screen: `THE BREATH BEFORE THE RACE.` → `GATHERING SOMETHING DEEPER.` → `THE ARDAS STARTS THE SAME WAY.`

segments.voice: The lines come from a poem by Guru Gobind Singh, the Var Sri Bhagauti Ji Ki, also called Chandi di Var, the ballad of Chandi. Its first stanza begins: pritham bhagauti simar kai, guru nanak laeen dhiai. In paraphrase: first, remember Bhagauti, then turn your mind to Guru Nanak. So the order of the whole Ardas starts here: first the Power, then the Gurus. Now, that word. In Punjabi, a bhagauti can be a sword. Because of that, Sikh readers understand Bhagauti here as God seen as power: the Timeless One whose strength cuts through injustice and fear, with the sword as its sign. The Khalsa's double-edged khanda and the kirpan carry the same idea. Other readers notice that the ballad goes on to tell the battles of the goddess Chandi from old Indian tales, and they hear Bhagauti as the goddess. Sikh teaching, and the way the Ardas is prayed, hold to the one God. Scholars also discuss how the Dasam Granth's poems were compiled. The words of the line, though, are the same for everyone: first, remember. Why put power first, before the Gurus, before any request? One answer Sikhs give: the Ardas is said by a community that has needed courage, under persecution, on battlefields, in prisons. Starting with the Power reminds the one praying that strength isn't something they have to manufacture. It's something to remember, the way a sprinter remembers what her legs can do. And there's a quiet humility in it: you begin a prayer not with yourself, but with what's greater than you.

segments.voice: Sit tall, feet flat on the floor, and notice where strength already lives in you: your spine holding you up, your lungs filling without being asked. You didn't make any of that; let yourself remember it, the way the Ardas remembers before it asks. If you pray, say Waheguru on each out-breath, as a way of remembering where the strength comes from.
Bhagauti. The sword, and the Power it stands for: in the Ardas, God remembered first, before anything is asked.
Your line: first, remember. Strength is something you remember, not something you make. Until tomorrow.

614.title: Nanak and Angad
614.hook: the Ardas remembers Guru Nanak, then Guru Angad
614.howItsDone: In every Ardas, after Bhagauti, Sikhs remember Guru Nanak and then Guru Angad by name, the first two in the line of ten Gurus.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Bhagauti, and your line: first, remember the Power. Today the Ardas turns from the Power to the people: the first two Gurus.

A family business, and the founder is getting old. Everyone assumes the son will take over: that's how it's always done. Then the founder chooses someone else. Not a relative. A man who came to visit and stayed, who did whatever he was asked, however odd, without arguing. The sons are not pleased. The town talks. It could be a story about a shop or a farm. Sikhs tell it about the very first handover of the Guruship, and the Ardas, every time it's prayed, says those two names in a row.
screen: `THE FOUNDER IS GETTING OLD.` → `HE CHOOSES SOMEONE ELSE.` → `THE FIRST HANDOVER.`

segments.voice: After first remembering the Power, the stanza goes on: guru nanak laeen dhiai, turn your mind to Guru Nanak. Then, phir angad gur te: then to Guru Angad. Guru Nanak needs little introduction by now. Born in the village now called Nankana Sahib, he traveled widely, sang the hymns that open the Guru Granth Sahib, and settled at Kartarpur, where a community farmed, ate together and sang. Near the end of his life came the handover. His disciple was a man named Lehna. Sikh tradition tells of tests: tasks that looked pointless or unpleasant, which others refused and Lehna simply did. Guru Nanak gave him a new name: Angad. Ang means a limb, a part of the body. Tradition hears the name as: you are a part of me. Guru Nanak had sons, and he passed them over. The Guruship would go by fitness, not by blood, and Sikhs see that choice as one of the founding moments of the faith. Guru Angad is remembered for quieter things. Tradition credits him with shaping and spreading the Gurmukhi script, the letters the scripture is written in. His wife, Mata Khivi, is remembered for running the langar with great generosity; she is named in the Guru Granth Sahib itself, where the bards Satta and Balwand praise her kitchen. And he collected Guru Nanak's hymns. So when the Ardas says Nanak, then Angad, it isn't just a list. It's the moment a teacher became a lineage, and, as Sikhs say, the same light passed from one person to another.
screen: `TURN YOUR MIND TO GURU NANAK.` · `LEHNA BECOMES ANGAD: A PART OF ME.` · `FITNESS, NOT BLOOD.` · `GURMUKHI, AND MATA KHIVI'S LANGAR.` · then, large: `NANAK, ANGAD.`

segments.voice: On one out-breath, say Nanak, and let a picture come with it: a traveler, a farmer at Kartarpur, a man singing. On the next, say Angad, and picture someone doing an odd, humble task without complaint; go back and forth, slowly, letting the names become a rhythm. If you pray, add Waheguru between them; if you don't, think of someone who passed something good on to you.
Angad. Guru Nanak's disciple, whom he named a part of himself: the first handover of the Guruship.
Your line: nanak, angad. One light, passed from a teacher to a disciple. See you tomorrow.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Angad, and your line: nanak, angad, the first handover. Today the same line of the Ardas names the third and fourth Gurus.

Most people, at seventy-three, are slowing down. Sikh tradition tells of a man who, at that age, was still carrying water before dawn, every day, for his teacher. One stormy night, the story goes, he stumbled and fell into a weaver's pit, and the weaver's wife laughed at the homeless old man. Not long after, that old man became the third Guru. And the young man he would later choose was another servant, an orphan who had sold boiled grain on the street as a boy. Two people the world overlooked. The Ardas names them together, and asks them for something.
screen: `SEVENTY-THREE, AND STILL CARRYING WATER.` → `A STREET SELLER, ORPHANED.` → `TWO PEOPLE THE WORLD OVERLOOKED.`

segments.voice: The Ardas line runs on from Angad: amar daas, raam daasai, hoeen sahai. Amar Das and Ram Das: be our help. Notice that verb. The Ardas doesn't just remember these two; it asks them to stand by us. Sahai, the helper, is a word we met in the saloks: You alone are the helper. Guru Amar Das became Guru in 1552, already in his seventies, after years of serving Guru Angad. He's remembered for making the langar a rule: pehle pangat, phir sangat, first sit in the line and eat, then join the gathering. Rich or poor, high caste or low, everyone sat on the same floor. Tradition says even the emperor Akbar sat in that line before meeting him. He organized the growing community into regions with appointed leaders, built a stepped well at Goindwal, and spoke against practices that harmed women, including sati. Guru Ram Das, born Jetha, was the orphan who sold grain. He came to Goindwal, served in the kitchen, married the Guru's daughter, Bibi Bhani, and became the fourth Guru in 1574. He founded the town that grew into Amritsar and began the pool at its heart. And he wrote the Lavan, the four verses of every Sikh wedding, sung as the couple walks around the Guru Granth Sahib. So these two names carry a kitchen floor where everyone is equal, a city and a wedding hymn. Both men began as servants. That's the pattern the Ardas keeps reminding Sikhs of: the ones who served became the ones who help.
screen: `AMAR DAS, RAM DAS: BE OUR HELP.` · `PEHLE PANGAT: FIRST, THE SHARED FLOOR.` · `RAM DAS: A CITY AND THE LAVAN.` · `THE SERVANTS BECAME THE HELP.` · then, large: `AMAR DAS, RAM DAS.`

segments.voice: Let the names ride on the in-breath: Amar Das, and an old man with a water pot in the dark; then Ram Das, and a young man stirring a pot in a crowded kitchen, with each out-breath long and empty between them. If you pray, add the Ardas's own words, hoeen sahai, be our help. If you don't, think of someone whose quiet service you've overlooked.
Amar Das. The third Guru, a servant first; the Ardas asks him, hoeen sahai, be our help.
Your line: amar das, ram das. Two servants, and now the Ardas asks them for help. Day six hundred fifteen.

616.title: Arjan and Hargobind
616.hook: then Guru Arjan and Guru Hargobind
616.howItsDone: In every Ardas Sikhs remember Guru Arjan and Guru Hargobind; Guru Arjan's martyrdom is marked each year, often with chhabeels serving cold drinks to passersby, and Bandi Chhor Divas recalls Guru Hargobind's release.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Amar Das, and your line: amar das, ram das. This week closed the ninth Guru's bani and opened the Ardas. Today, a father and a son.

Lahore. A man is held by the authorities and dies after being tortured. Sikh tradition remembers him sitting calm through it, saying God's will is sweet. He is the Guru, and his son is still a boy. What does a boy do with that? This one, tradition says, put on two swords. Then he built a raised platform facing the Harmandir Sahib. The father had built a house for the scripture. The son built a seat for the community's courage.
screen: `LAHORE.` → `HIS SON IS STILL A BOY.` → `TWO SWORDS, AND A RAISED SEAT.`

segments.voice: The Ardas line goes: arjan hargobind no simrau. Remember Arjan and Hargobind. Guru Arjan, the fifth Guru, was the son of Guru Ram Das. He finished the pool at Amritsar and built the Harmandir Sahib in its middle, with doors on all four sides, open to everyone from every direction. He compiled the Adi Granth, gathering the hymns of the Gurus before him, his own, and the hymns of saints from other backgrounds, Hindu and Muslim, and installed it in the Harmandir. He wrote the Sukhmani Sahib, the Psalm of Peace, which we read earlier this year. And he was executed in Lahore under the emperor Jahangir. Sikhs remember him as the first Sikh martyr. Tradition remembers him living out a line of his own bani, which Sikhs often say as tera bhana meetha laage: Your will is sweet. Guru Hargobind, his son, became Guru as a boy. Tradition says he wore two swords, one called miri, for worldly responsibility, and one called piri, for the spiritual. And he built the Akal Takht, the Throne of the Timeless, facing the Harmandir: a seat of community authority beside the house of prayer. Later he was held in Gwalior fort; Sikhs remember his release, along with fifty-two imprisoned princes, on Bandi Chhor Divas, which falls with Diwali. The father built the house and the book, and gave his life quietly. The son added the sword and the throne, so the community could stand. The Ardas holds both in one breath: the calm and the courage, the scripture and the seat.
screen: `ARJAN: THE HOUSE AND THE BOOK.` · `REMEMBERED AS THE FIRST SIKH MARTYR.` · `HARGOBIND: MIRI AND PIRI.` · `THE CALM AND THE COURAGE.` · then, large: `ARJAN, HARGOBIND.`

segments.voice: Hands open on your knees, on a long out-breath, say Arjan, calm like four open doors; then sit a little taller, close your hands gently, and say Hargobind, steady like someone standing up straight. If you pray, say tera bhana meetha laage, Your will is sweet, after them; if you don't, think about where you need calm today, and where you need courage.
Miri piri, worldly and spiritual authority. Guru Hargobind wore the two swords, miri and piri, after his father Guru Arjan, the first Sikh martyr, built the house and the book.
Your line: arjan, hargobind. The calm and the courage, held in one breath. Until tomorrow.
